column3: Brief Description
Build a small audio tool that reduces steady background noise such as fan or hum noise. Compare simple time-domain smoothing with frequency-domain filtering and let the user hear the result.
Create a basic equalizer with low-, mid-, and high-frequency controls. Use the FFT or simple filters to change frequency bands and display the spectrum before and after.
Add adjustable echo and simple room-like reverb to a voice or music clip. Model each effect as convolution with a short impulse response.
Make a simple editor that can trim, join, reverse, scale, and fade audio clips. Show the waveform and include one convolution-based effect such as smoothing or echo.
Mark the portions of a recording that contain speech and the portions that are silent. Use short-time energy and simple thresholds, with plots that explain each decision.
Estimate the main pitch of a sung or played note. Compare a time-domain method such as autocorrelation with the largest peak in the frequency spectrum.
Estimate the tempo of a short music clip by finding repeated energy peaks. Display the detected beats on the waveform and report beats per minute.
Recognize the two tones produced by telephone keypad buttons. Use the DFT or FFT to find the strongest low- and high-frequency components and identify each digit.
Decode a clean audio recording of Morse code into dots, dashes, and text. Use filtering, envelope detection, and timing thresholds.
Record a few simple sounds, such as a clap, bell, or tap, and recognize them by comparing short spectra or correlations with saved examples.
Let users change playback speed and explore how naive resampling also changes pitch. Add a simple option that changes the sampling rate and clearly demonstrates aliasing.
Turn a sound clip into a time-frequency image using short overlapping FFT windows. Let the user change window size and observe the trade-off between time and frequency detail.
Detect and reduce 50 Hz electrical hum and its nearby components in an audio recording. Display the unwanted spectral peak and the cleaned waveform.
Reduce very loud portions of an audio clip while keeping quiet parts audible. Plot the input-output amplitude rule and compare the waveform before and after.
Analyze a recorded or sample pulse/heartbeat signal by smoothing it, finding peaks, and estimating heart rate. Clearly state that it is an educational analyzer, not a medical tool.
Use phone accelerometer data to count steps and study periodic motion. Apply smoothing, peak detection, and a frequency plot to estimate walking pace.
Analyze vibration data from a phone or a small sensor. Show dominant frequencies and warn when vibration energy rises above a user-set threshold.
Simulate a simple beam or ruler vibrating as a mixture of a few sinusoidal modes. Use Fourier components to show how different modes combine into the observed motion.
Record a clap in a room and estimate its echo delay and decay. Use correlation and a simple impulse-response view to compare two rooms or locations.
Simulate sending a short pulse and receiving a delayed echo. Estimate distance from the delay and study how noise and filtering affect the estimate.
Apply blur and sharpening kernels to an image using 2D convolution. Let users edit a small kernel and immediately see how it changes the result.
Find horizontal, vertical, and combined edges using small convolution kernels. Compare several kernels and display both the filtered image and edge strength.
Add salt-and-pepper or Gaussian-like noise to an image and try simple cleaning filters. Compare the visual result and a basic error measure.
Compute a 2D DFT of an image and let users suppress or keep selected frequency regions. Reconstruct the image and explain how low and high frequencies affect appearance.
Keep only the largest DFT coefficients of an image and reconstruct it. Plot file-size or coefficient-count reduction against reconstruction quality.
Resize an image using nearest-neighbor and linear interpolation. Include anti-aliasing before downsampling and compare the visible differences.
Create motion blur by convolving an image with a line-shaped kernel. Add a limited restoration attempt using a known blur kernel and discuss where it fails.
Compare simple textures such as cloth, brick, or grass using their 2D frequency patterns. Report dominant directions or repeating spacing without using machine learning.
Create an interactive grid where users draw a tiny image and a kernel, then watch every multiply-and-add step of 2D convolution.
Separate an image into red, green, and blue signals and compare their histograms and frequency content. Add simple per-channel smoothing or sharpening.
Detect repeated stripes or grid spacing in an image from peaks in its 2D spectrum. Test the method on generated patterns and a few real images.
Extract or accept the boundary points of a simple shape and analyze the x- and y-coordinate signals. Compare shapes using a small set of Fourier descriptors.
Let users draw a one-dimensional signal and approximate it using a selected number of Fourier-series terms. Show each component and the reconstruction error.
Animate discrete or continuous convolution by flipping, shifting, multiplying, and summing two signals. Include common examples such as pulses and decaying exponentials.
Let users enter an input signal and an impulse response, then compute the output by convolution. Check simple properties such as causality and stability from the impulse response.
Build simple low-pass, high-pass, and band-pass filters from adjustable coefficients. Show the impulse response, frequency response, pole-zero plot, and filtered output.
Solve a small linear constant-coefficient differential equation using the Laplace transform. Plot the zero-input, zero-state, and total responses for simple inputs.
Simulate a discrete-time system defined by a linear difference equation. Use the Z-transform or direct recursion and compare the two results.
Sample a generated continuous-looking signal and reconstruct it with zero-order hold, linear interpolation, and sinc-like interpolation. Compare errors at several sampling rates.
Create a simple amplitude-modulated signal, display its spectrum, add noise, and recover the message using envelope detection and low-pass filtering.
Send a sequence of rectangular pulses through a noisy channel and recover the bits. Use convolution for the channel, a matched filter or correlation, and threshold detection.
Treat a clean one-dimensional barcode scan as a signal, smooth it, find transitions, and decode a small custom barcode format. Study the effect of blur and sampling rate.
Analyze a time series of vehicle counts from a road or generated dataset. Smooth noise, find daily or weekly periodicity with the FFT, and flag unusual peaks.

Create a tool that hides a short message by nudging selected 2D CFT coefficients of an image and a matching extractor that reads the message back from the perturbed spectrum. Test how well extraction survives noise, cropping, and rescaling attacks.

column2: Antenna and Speaker Array Beam Pattern Designer
column3: Design a phased array by setting the number of elements, spacing, and per-element amplitude/phase, then compute and plot the far-field directivity pattern as the Fourier transform of the aperture. Add a steering control and show the total pattern as the convolution of the element pattern with the array factor.

Estimate the translation between two shifted images using phase correlation: compute the 2D CFT of each image, form the normalized cross-power spectrum, and inverse-transform to find the shift from the correlation peak. Display the recovered shift and the aligned overlay.

column2:
Fourier-Domain Image Encryptor 
(Double Random Phase Encoding)
column3: Encrypt an image using Double Random Phase Encoding: multiply the image by a random phase mask, take its 2D CFT, multiply the result by a second random phase mask, and inverse-transform to produce noise-like ciphertext. Build the matching decryptor that only recovers the original with the correct pair of secret phase-key images, and show that a slightly wrong key yields pure noise.

Change the pitch of an audio clip independently of its playback speed (or vice versa) using STFT frame analysis with phase-coherent overlap-add reconstruction, the real technique behind vocal pitch-shifting tools. Compare the phase-corrected result against naive resampling to show why phase continuity matters.

Simulate how MRI machines build images: sample a target image's 2D CFT (k-space) along a chosen trajectory such as full grid, radial, or random undersampling, then reconstruct via the inverse 2D CFT. Compare resolution loss and artifacts produced by different sampling patterns and undersampling rates.

Given a target image, compute a phase-only pattern using iterative phase retrieval (alternating forward and inverse 2D CFT) so that Fourier-transforming the pattern reproduces the target image, the principle behind laser-projector holograms and beam shaping. Simulate the optical reconstruction and plot error against the number of iterations.

Fit the dominant Fourier Series harmonics of a periodic real-world series such as electricity load, sales, or traffic counts, subtract them to obtain a deseasonalized trend, and forecast forward by re-adding the fitted seasonal component to an extrapolated trend. Evaluate forecast accuracy against held-out data.

Fit dominant Fourier-series harmonics to a periodic real-world time series, such as electricity load, sales, or traffic counts. Remove the fitted seasonal component to obtain a deseasonalized trend, forecast the trend forward, then add the seasonal component back. Evaluate the forecast on held-out data and visualize the original signal, fitted harmonics, trend, and prediction.

Build an audio-processing tool where users upload or record a short audio clip, visualize its waveform and frequency spectrum, and interactively “cut” selected frequency ranges using draggable frequency-band scissors. The modified audio will be reconstructed using the inverse Fourier transform so users can hear how removing, attenuating, or amplifying different frequency bands changes the sound. The project should compare the original and processed audio through waveform plots, spectra, and listening tests, demonstrating practical frequency-domain filtering and audio editing.
